nameStory: The 'redroot' in this sedge's name tells you exactly what makes it special among New England's flatsedges. When you carefully dig up this plant, you'll discover bright red roots that are absolutely unique among all North American flatsedges. Both the scientific name 'erythrorhizos' (meaning red roots in Greek) and the common name celebrate this distinctive underground feature.
description: Redroot flatsedge is an annual sedge that grows in dense clumps, typically reaching 6-24 inches tall. Like other sedges, it has triangular stems and narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge from the base. The plant produces small, brownish flower clusters at the top of its stems in umbrella-like arrangements. What makes this species truly special is hidden underground - those brilliant red roots that no other North American flatsedge can claim.

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Bright red roots that feel firm and fibrous when gently examined - this is the only North American flatsedge with this vivid coloring

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Triangular stems that feel distinctly three-sided when rolled between your fingers, typical of all sedges

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small brownish flower clusters arranged in umbrella-like groups at stem tips, with thin, leaf-like bracts extending beyond the flowers

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that emerge from the base and feel smooth along the edges, unlike many grasses which can feel rough

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense clumps in wet areas, with multiple stems growing close together from the same root system

habitat: Look for redroot flatsedge in wet, muddy soils along pond edges, stream banks, and in marshy areas throughout New England. It thrives in seasonally flooded spots and disturbed wetland edges where the soil stays moist but isn't permanently underwater. You'll often find it growing alongside other moisture-loving plants like rushes and other sedges.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small tufts of narrow green leaves, with the distinctive red roots already present if you gently examine the base.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with full-sized clumps and brownish flower clusters appearing at stem tips from mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse while the above-ground parts begin to yellow and die back as this annual completes its life cycle.
seasonality.winter: The annual plants have died completely, leaving only seeds to sprout the following spring in suitable wet soil conditions.

funFact: Redroot flatsedge is like nature's own mood ring - those brilliant red roots are so unique that if you find any North American flatsedge with red roots, you can be 100% certain of its identity without even looking at the flowers or leaves!
confusionNotes: Redroot flatsedge can easily be confused with other flatsedges and even young grasses when growing in wetlands, but the red roots are your foolproof identifier. Remember: 'Red roots, right answer' - no other flatsedge in North America has this feature. Above ground, look for the triangular stems (sedges have edges!) versus round grass stems.
contextualKnowledge: Like all sedges, this plant belongs to the group remembered by the old botanist's rhyme: 'Sedges have edges, rushes are round, grasses have joints when the stems can be found.' The triangular stem is your first clue you're looking at a sedge rather than a grass, even before you check those telltale red roots.
compareHints: Among its many flatsedge cousins in New England, redroot flatsedge stands alone with those brilliant red roots - no other Cyperus species has this feature. Yellow nutsedge has yellowish tubers, straw-colored flatsedge has pale roots, and all the others have whitish or brownish root systems. If you see red underground, you've found your redroot flatsedge.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many flatsedge species, straw-colored flatsedge stands out for its relatively tall height and branching, airy flower clusters.

Among New England's flatsedges, yellow nutsedge is distinctive for its bright golden-yellow flowers and robust growth habit - most other flatsedges have brownish or straw-colored flowers and are generally smaller.
Among New England's flatsedges, toothed flatsedge is unique in reliably producing bulblets, which sets it apart from relatives like yellow nutsedge or straw-colored flatsedge.
Among its flatsedge relatives, shining flatsedge stands out for its particularly glossy flower scales - most other Cyperus species have duller, more matte-colored scales.

Among New England's many flatsedges, Great Plains flatsedge is distinguished by its compact, clumping growth habit and relatively small size compared to the taller, more sprawling straw-colored flatsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, bearded flatsedge is distinguished by its prominently bristly flower clusters that truly look bearded.

Among New England's flatsedges, Engelmann's is distinguished by its relatively small size and compact flower clusters compared to the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or the more robust yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, umbrella flatsedge stays notably short and compact compared to the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or yellow nutsedge.
Among its flatsedge relatives, small-flower halfchaff sedge is distinguished by its particularly tiny flower clusters and more delicate build.
Among New England's flatsedges, Gray's is distinguished by its relatively large size and the specific arrangement of its flower clusters.
Asian flatsedge is smaller and more delicate than most of its flatsedge relatives like straw-colored flatsedge or yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's many flatsedges, fern flatsedge stands out for its particularly delicate, finely-branched flower clusters that are more lacy and open than most relatives.
Among New England's flatsedges, fragrant flatsedge is distinguished by its sweet scent when crushed and its preference for consistently moist soils.

Among New England's flatsedges, variable flatsedge is distinguished by its very compact, ball-like flower clusters rather than the loose, umbrella-shaped arrangements of umbrella flatsedge or the elongated spikes of yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, brown flatsedge is distinguished by its rich chocolate-brown flower clusters - most other flatsedges have yellow, straw-colored, or greenish flowers.
Rice flat-sedge is smaller and more delicate than most of its flatsedge relatives in New England, such as the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or the robust yellow nutsedge.
Among its flatsedge relatives, Houghton's Umbrella-sedge is distinguished by its small size and preference for sandy lake shores rather than muddy wetlands.
Yellow flatsedge is much smaller and more delicate than its relatives like yellow nutsedge, which has underground tubers, or straw-colored flatsedge, which grows much taller.
Among its flatsedge relatives, Asiatic greenhead sedge is notably smaller and more compact than yellow nutsedge or straw-colored flatsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, Globe Flatsedge stands out for its perfectly round, compact flower clusters - most others like Yellow Nutsedge have more open, branched arrangements.
Japanese flatsedge is generally smaller and more compact than the common yellow flatsedge, and lacks the distinctive straw-colored appearance of straw-colored flatsedge.
Pinebarren flatsedge is shorter and has cylindrical flower clusters compared to most of its flatsedge relatives.
